day_by_day.morning: N/A – Flight TP arrives at 13:00. Use the morning to rest on the plane and prepare for arrival.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive at Lisbon Airport at 13:00. Take the Metro (Line Vermelha/Red Line) from Aeroporto station directly into the city – cheapest option at ~€1.65 with a Viva Viagem card. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up. Spend the rest of the afternoon taking a relaxed orientation walk through the Baixa (Downtown) district – stroll Rua Augusta, admire the Praça do Comércio waterfront square, and soak in your first views of the Tagus River. Entry to the square is free.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the Alfama district (a short tram or walk from Baixa) for your first evening. Explore the narrow medieval streets at dusk and listen for Fado music drifting from local tascas. Grab dinner at a no-frills local tasca on the hillside.

meals.breakfast: On the plane or grab a pastel de nata and espresso (called 'bica') at a café near the airport or hotel for under €2.
meals.lunch: Pick up a fresh sandwich (prego no pão – steak roll) or a bifana from a local snack bar near Baixa for €3–5.
meals.dinner: Dinner at a local tasca in Alfama – look for the 'prato do dia' (dish of the day), typically €7–10 including bread, olives, and a drink. Try bacalhau à brás (salt cod with eggs and potatoes).

day_by_day.notes: Buy a 7-day Viva Viagem rechargeable Metro/bus card at the airport (€0.50 for the card + load credit). This will save money all week. Keep luggage light on the Metro – it can get busy. Alfama streets are hilly and cobblestoned, so wear comfortable shoes.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) – one of Lisbon's most unique and rewarding museums. Explore five centuries of Portuguese azulejo (decorative tile) art housed in a stunning former convent. Entry is €5 (discounted or free with certain EU cards). Open from 10:00. Reach it by Bus 794 or Tram 28E from the city center.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the historic Mouraria and Graça neighborhoods – the oldest and most authentic quarters of Lisbon. Climb to the Miradouro da Graça viewpoint for panoramic city views (free). Then walk down to the Castelo de São Jorge (St. George's Castle). Entrance is €15 full price, but you can enjoy excellent free views of the castle exterior and the surrounding streets without going inside to save budget.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for a proper Fado evening. Many small restaurants host live Fado performances with dinner – look for spots with no minimum spend or a modest cover charge (€5–10). Alternatively, some tascas offer free Fado on weekends. Enjoy a glass of house wine (vinho da casa) for €1–2.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel or a local padaria (bakery) – coffee and pastel de nata for €1.50–2.50.
meals.lunch: Lunch near the Tile Museum or Mouraria – try a local café offering a 'menu do dia' (set lunch: soup + main + drink) for €8–10.
meals.dinner: Dinner at a Fado tasca in Alfama – budget €12–15 for a full meal with house wine. Ask locals for non-touristy recommendations.

day_by_day.notes: The National Tile Museum is closed on Mondays, so Saturday is perfect. Wear comfortable shoes – Alfama and Graça involve steep hills and cobblestones. Carry a light jacket as evenings can be cool in May.

day_by_day.morning: Take the train from Cais do Sodré station to Belém (free with Viva Viagem card top-up, ~€1.65 each way, 15 minutes). Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery – a breathtaking example of Manueline architecture. Entrance to the church is free; the cloisters cost €10 (worth it) or €16 combined with the Tower of Belém. Arrive early to beat crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk along Belém's riverside promenade to the iconic Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém) – another Manueline masterpiece and UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entry €6 (or combined ticket). Also stroll past the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) along the waterfront – exterior viewing is free. After sightseeing, make the essential pilgrimage to Pastéis de Belém bakery (the original since 1837) for the famous custard tarts – €1.20–1.50 each. Expect a short queue but it moves fast.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon. Explore the trendy LX Factory (open Sundays with a popular market) – a repurposed industrial space with street art, local vendors, food stalls, and bars. Great for picking up affordable local snacks and soaking up Lisbon's creative scene.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and toast at a café near the hotel before heading to Belém – budget €2–3.
meals.lunch: Grab a snack lunch near Belém – the famous pastéis de nata from Pastéis de Belém plus a bifana or sandwich from a nearby café for under €8 total.
meals.dinner: Dinner at LX Factory on Sunday – explore the food stalls and pick affordable plates (€8–12). Try local street food like grilled sardines or chouriço bread.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6km west of central Lisbon – the train from Cais do Sodré is the easiest and cheapest option. The Jerónimos Monastery and Tower of Belém are close together and walkable. LX Factory's Sunday market runs roughly 10:00–20:00 – great for late afternoon browsing.

day_by_day.morning: Spend the morning at the Time Out Market Food Tour experience – Lisbon's iconic food hall in the Cais do Sodré area. Sample the best of Portuguese cuisine from top chefs and local producers, including bacalhau dishes, petiscos (Portuguese tapas), ginjinha (cherry liqueur), and more. Even without a formal tour, the market is free to enter and you can graze on small dishes. Budget €15–20 for a satisfying food exploration.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Chiado and Bairro Alto neighborhoods – Lisbon's cultural and bohemian heart. Visit the free Igreja do Carmo (Carmo Church ruins – a hauntingly beautiful roofless Gothic church destroyed in the 1755 earthquake; entry ~€5). Browse independent bookshops including the historic Livraria Bertrand (world's oldest operating bookshop – free to enter). Ride the iconic Elevador da Bica or Elevador da Glória funicular for €3.80 (or walk up for free) for great city views.
day_by_day.evening: Stroll through Príncipe Real neighborhood – a charming upscale-but-relaxed area with a lovely garden square. Enjoy sunset views from Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara (free viewpoint in Bairro Alto). End the evening with dinner in Bairro Alto.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at a local café in Baixa – galão (milky coffee) and a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese) for €3–4.
meals.lunch: Graze at the Time Out Market – budget €12–18 for multiple small tastings including a drink.
meals.dinner: Dinner at a petiscos (tapas-style) restaurant in Bairro Alto – order 3–4 small shared dishes for €10–14 per person with a glass of wine.

day_by_day.notes: Monday is a good day for Chiado and Bairro Alto as many shops and restaurants are open. Note that some museums are closed on Mondays (already accounted for in this itinerary). The Time Out Market is open daily from 10:00. Bairro Alto's restaurant scene comes alive after 19:00.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) – Portugal's most important art museum housing masterpieces from the 12th–19th centuries including Nuno Gonçalves' famous polyptych panels. Entry is €6 (free on Sunday mornings until 14:00 – note this for future reference). Located in the Santos neighborhood, reachable by bus or a scenic walk along the river from Cais do Sodré.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Parque das Nações (Park of Nations) district – built for Expo '98 and now a modern riverside neighborhood with free public spaces, futuristic architecture, and the Tagus riverfront promenade. Walk the boardwalk, admire the Cable Car (skip the ride to save budget – €4 each way), and visit the free exterior of the stunning Oriente Train Station (designed by Santiago Calatrava). The Oceanarium is here too (€21) – skip for budget reasons unless it's a priority.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon for a final evening. Head to Intendente square – a multicultural, authentic neighborhood that's off the typical tourist trail. Browse the local shops and end your trip with a farewell dinner at a traditional Portuguese restaurant. Toast to your Lisbon adventure with a glass of Vinho Verde or a shot of ginjinha from a street kiosk (€1.50).

meals.breakfast: Final hotel breakfast or local café – pastel de nata and bica for €2.
meals.lunch: Lunch in Parque das Nações – grab a prato do dia at a local café for €8–10, or pick up food from a supermarket (Continente or Pingo Doce nearby) for a budget picnic by the river (€5–7).
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a traditional tasca in Intendente or Anjos neighborhood – full meal with wine for €12–15. Try caldo verde (green soup), grilled fish, and a pastel de nata for dessert.

day_by_day.notes: Parque das Nações is best reached by Metro (Red Line to Oriente station – same line as the airport). If your departure flight is on May 20th, pack your bags tonight and confirm transport to the airport (Metro Red Line from Oriente or Alameda station – about 20–30 minutes, €1.65). Keep your Viva Viagem card topped up for the airport journey home.

trip_options.title: Classic Lisbon, Portugal Experience
trip_options.description: The sweet spot between comfort and value. Enjoy quality accommodations, diverse experiences, and good food.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival — Flight TP lands at 13:00, so no morning activities. Take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) from Humberto Delgado Airport to central Lisbon (~35 min, €2–4). Check in to Lisbon City Stay, freshen up, and get oriented in the neighborhood.
day_by_day.afternoon: Take a leisurely stroll through Baixa-Chiado, Lisbon's elegant downtown grid. Walk along Rua Augusta, cross the iconic Praça do Comércio by the Tagus riverfront, and ride the historic Elevador de Santa Justa (€5.30) for panoramic rooftop views over the city. A gentle, low-effort way to shake off travel fatigue and get your bearings.
day_by_day.evening: Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show — Join an early-evening guided walking tour through Alfama's medieval alleyways, Moorish staircases, and miradouros (viewpoints). End the night with a traditional Fado performance at a local casa de fado, where Portugal's soulful music fills intimate tiled rooms.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and pastel de nata at a café near the airport or after check-in — try A Padaria Portuguesa near Baixa for a quick, authentic bite (€3–5).
meals.lunch: Light lunch at a tasca in Baixa-Chiado after settling in — try Zé da Mouraria or a similar neighborhood spot for a prato do dia (dish of the day) with soup, main, and drink for €10–13.
meals.dinner: Dinner included or adjacent to the Fado experience in Alfama. Look for tascas like Tasca do Chico or Solar dos Presuntos offering petiscos (Portuguese tapas) — budget €25–35 per person including wine.

day_by_day.notes: Keep Day 1 light — jet lag and travel fatigue are real. The Fado evening is best booked in advance, especially for weekends. Wear comfortable shoes as Alfama has steep, cobblestoned streets.

day_by_day.morning: Time Out Market Food Tour — Head to the iconic Mercado da Ribeira (Time Out Market) in Cais do Sodré for a late-morning food crawl. Sample the best of Portuguese cuisine: from bacalhau (salt cod) dishes and bifanas (pork sandwiches) to artisan cheeses, local wines, and ginjinha (cherry liqueur). This is a hands-on, delicious introduction to the country's food culture.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk or take Tram 28 to the Mouraria and Graça neighborhoods — explore the multicultural roots of Lisbon, visit the Castelo de São Jorge (€15) for sweeping city views and a deep dive into Lisbon's Moorish and medieval history. Wander the castle grounds at your own pace.
day_by_day.evening: Return to the Alfama/Mouraria area for a relaxed evening. Browse the Feira da Ladra flea market area (if stalls are still open late afternoon on Sunday), then settle into a local restaurant for a traditional Sunday dinner.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and toast with butter and jam (torrada) at a local café near the hotel — a classic Portuguese breakfast for €3–5.
meals.lunch: Covered by the Time Out Market Food Tour — graze on multiple stalls for €15–20 total, mixing savory bites and a glass of vinho verde.
meals.dinner: Tasca near Graça or Alfama — try Taberna da Rua das Flores or a neighborhood spot for caldo verde (green soup), grilled fish or roast lamb, and a local wine. Budget €20–28 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Time Out Market is busiest midday on Sundays — arrive by 10:30–11:00 to beat the crowds. Castelo de São Jorge can be warm in the afternoon sun; bring water and sunscreen. Tram 28 is charming but very crowded — consider walking or taking a Tuk-Tuk as an alternative.

day_by_day.morning: National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — Take the bus or a short Uber to this world-class museum housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. Spend 2–3 hours exploring five centuries of azulejo tile art, from Moorish geometric patterns to Baroque masterpieces and the famous 23-meter panoramic tile panel of pre-earthquake Lisbon. A must for history and art lovers.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Parque das Nações (Park of Nations), Lisbon's modern riverside district built for Expo '98. Stroll along the Tagus promenade, visit the striking Oriente train station (a masterpiece by Santiago Calatrava), and explore the contemporary architecture as a contrast to the city's ancient districts.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon — enjoy the vibrant Bairro Alto or Príncipe Real neighborhoods. Browse independent boutiques and bookshops, then settle in for dinner in Príncipe Real, one of Lisbon's most charming and locals-loved quarters.

meals.breakfast: Pastéis de nata and galão (milky espresso) at a local pastelaria near the hotel — €4–6.
meals.lunch: Lunch near the Tile Museum or Parque das Nações — try a riverside café in Parque das Nações for fresh fish or a bifana sandwich. Budget €12–16.
meals.dinner: Dinner in Príncipe Real — try Taberna da Rua das Flores or Pharmácia Restaurant for creative Portuguese cuisine in a beautiful setting. Budget €25–35 per person with wine.

day_by_day.notes: The Tile Museum is closed on Mondays — if this is an issue, swap with the Belém day. Double-check opening hours before visiting. Parque das Nações is easily reached via Metro (Red Line, Oriente station).

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Monuments & Pastéis de Belém — Take the tram or bus west along the Tagus to Belém. Start with the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery (€10), a breathtaking example of Manueline Gothic architecture built to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Explore the ornate cloisters and the tombs of Portuguese kings and explorers.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue in Belém — visit the iconic Torre de Belém (€6), the 16th-century riverside fortress and symbol of Portugal's Age of Discovery. Also stop at the Padrão dos Descobrimentos (Monument to the Discoveries, €4) for river views and historical context. End with the mandatory stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (since 1837) for the world's best custard tarts — €1.20 each.
day_by_day.evening: Head back toward central Lisbon and wind down in the Santos or Cais do Sodré neighborhood. Enjoy a sundowner at a riverside bar watching the light fade over the Tagus, then dinner in a nearby tasca.

meals.breakfast: Full Portuguese breakfast at a café near the hotel — eggs, toast, cheese, ham, juice, and coffee for €7–10.
meals.lunch: Lunch at a restaurant in Belém — try Vela Latina or a nearby tasca for fresh grilled fish and salad. Budget €15–20. Don't forget the pastéis de Belém for dessert!
meals.dinner: Dinner in Cais do Sodré or Santos — try Taberna Sal Grosso or a local petiscos bar for shared small plates and natural wine. Budget €20–28 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6–7 km from central Lisbon — Tram 15E or Bus 728 are the easiest options (€2 each way). Jerónimos Monastery can have queues; arrive early (opens at 10:00). The Pastéis de Belém bakery always has a line but moves quickly — worth the wait.

day_by_day.morning: Mercado de Campo de Ourique & Local Neighborhood Lunch — Take the tram or a short walk to Campo de Ourique, a quiet, authentic residential neighborhood beloved by locals. Explore the charming covered market (Mercado de Campo de Ourique), open since 1934, browsing stalls of fresh produce, cheeses, charcuterie, and flowers. Chat with vendors, pick up edible souvenirs, and soak up genuine Lisbon neighborhood life far from tourist crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: Free afternoon for personal exploration or last-minute shopping. Options include: browsing the antique shops and concept stores of Príncipe Real, visiting the Museu do Azulejo shop for tile souvenirs, walking through the Jardim da Estrela (beautiful public garden near Campo de Ourique) for a peaceful rest, or heading to Miradouro da Graça or Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for final panoramic views of the city.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner — treat yourself to a memorable final meal celebrating the best of Portuguese cuisine. Choose a well-regarded mid-range restaurant in Chiado or Bairro Alto for a full sit-down dinner with wine, finishing with a ginjinha at a traditional bar like A Ginjinha near Rossio.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the Mercado de Campo de Ourique — grab fresh pastries, fruit, and coffee from market stalls for a lively, local experience. €5–8.
meals.lunch: Lunch inside or around the Mercado de Campo de Ourique — the market has excellent food stalls. Try bacalhau à brás (shredded cod with eggs and potatoes) or a fresh seafood dish. Budget €12–16.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a Chiado restaurant — try Cantinho do Avillez (José Avillez's casual bistro) or Taberna da Rua das Flores for refined Portuguese cooking. Budget €30–40 per person with wine. End with a ginjinha at A Ginjinha (€1.50 a shot) — a Lisbon tradition.

day_by_day.notes: Campo de Ourique market is liveliest Tuesday–Saturday mornings. Pack any ceramic or tile souvenirs carefully — bubble wrap is available at most shops. If flying out soon, confirm your departure logistics from Lisbon City Stay to the airport (Metro is easiest, ~35 min).

highlights: Mix of paid and free experiences

day_by_day.morning: No morning activities — flight TP arrives at 13:00. Transfer from Lisbon Humberto Delgado Airport to Lisbon City Stay via private luxury transfer. Check in, freshen up, and settle into your accommodation.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely stroll through the nearby streets to get your bearings. Visit the iconic Time Out Market (Mercado da Ribeira) for a curated first taste of Lisbon — sample petiscos, fresh seafood, and artisan cheeses from Portugal's top chefs. A perfect, relaxed introduction to local food culture without overwhelming jet-lagged senses.
day_by_day.evening: Head to the elegant Bairro Alto or Chiado neighborhood for a premium dinner. Dine at Belcanto (two Michelin stars, Chef José Avillez) for a refined contemporary Portuguese tasting menu — one of Lisbon's most celebrated culinary experiences. Book well in advance. After dinner, enjoy a glass of aged port at a nearby wine bar such as By the Wine.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast on the plane or a light snack upon arrival at the hotel — most luxury hotels offer a welcome amenity tray.
meals.lunch: Time Out Market: graze on a curated selection of stalls — try Henrique Sá Pessoa's counter, fresh oysters, and a pastel de nata to finish. Budget €30–50 per person.
meals.dinner: Belcanto Restaurant, Rua Serpa Pinto 10A — tasting menu from €200 per person. Alternatively, Alma (one Michelin star) for a slightly more relaxed but equally premium experience.

day_by_day.notes: Arrival day — keep the schedule flexible and low-stress. Confirm your Belcanto reservation months in advance as tables are extremely limited. Private airport transfer recommended for a seamless luxury arrival experience.

day_by_day.morning: Begin the day with a full Portuguese breakfast at your hotel or at Café A Brasileira, one of Lisbon's most storied historic cafés in Chiado — espresso, fresh pastries, and local cheeses. Then embark on the Alfama District Walking Tour: explore the oldest neighborhood in Lisbon with a private expert guide, winding through medieval alleyways, past Moorish-influenced architecture, the Sé Cathedral, and up to the São Jorge Castle for panoramic views over the city and the Tagus River.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the tour, visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — a world-class institution housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. Spend 1.5–2 hours exploring five centuries of Portuguese azulejo tile artistry, including the remarkable 23-metre panoramic tile panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon. The museum itself is a masterpiece of architecture and heritage.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for an authentic Fado Show dinner experience — the perfect cultural capstone to a day immersed in Lisbon's history. Reserve a table at Clube de Fado or Mesa de Frades, both intimate, premium venues where world-class fadistas perform in candlelit settings. Dinner includes traditional Portuguese dishes such as bacalhau à brás, slow-roasted lamb, and local wines.

meals.breakfast: Café A Brasileira, Rua Garrett 120, Chiado — galão coffee, croissants, and local cheese. €10–15 per person.
meals.lunch: Light lunch near the Tile Museum at Solar dos Presuntos or a nearby tasca — petiscos, charcuterie, and regional wines. €40–60 per person.
meals.dinner: Mesa de Frades, Rua dos Remédios 139A — intimate Fado dinner in a converted chapel. Expect to spend €80–120 per person including wine and the Fado performance. Reservations essential.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Fado dinner well in advance — premium venues like Mesa de Frades have very limited seating. The Alfama walking tour is best enjoyed in the morning before the afternoon heat and tourist crowds peak. Wear comfortable walking shoes as the cobblestone streets are steep.

day_by_day.morning: Dedicate the morning to the magnificent Belém district, a 20-minute taxi or Uber ride from central Lisbon. Begin with a visit to the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery — a breathtaking example of Manueline architecture commissioned to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Explore the ornate cloisters, the church, and the tombs of Portugal's greatest explorers. Arrive early (opens at 9:30am) to beat the crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk along the Tagus riverfront to the iconic Tower of Belém — another Manueline masterpiece and symbol of Portugal's Age of Discovery. Then make your way to the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) for the original, irreplaceable pastel de nata — warm, dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar. Afterward, visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) for additional historical context and river views. Consider a private guided commentary for deeper historical insight.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and dine at Eleven Restaurant (Michelin-starred), perched above Parque Eduardo VII with sweeping city views. Chef Joachim Koerper delivers refined Mediterranean-Portuguese cuisine in a sleek, contemporary setting — ideal for a premium evening. After dinner, enjoy a nightcap at Topo Chiado rooftop bar for panoramic night views over Lisbon's illuminated skyline.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast or a stop at Pastelaria Versailles in Belém for a traditional Portuguese breakfast before the monastery opens.
meals.lunch: Pastéis de Belém for the iconic pastry experience, followed by a proper lunch at Solar dos Bacalhaus or Taberna da Rua das Flores — traditional bacalhau dishes in a premium setting. €50–70 per person.
meals.dinner: Eleven Restaurant, Rua Marquês da Fronteira — tasting menu from €120–160 per person. Stunning views and impeccable service.

day_by_day.notes: Jerónimos Monastery is closed on Mondays — Sunday is ideal. Purchase skip-the-line tickets online in advance. The Belém area is best explored on foot along the riverside promenade. A private driver for the day to and from Belém adds comfort and flexibility.

day_by_day.morning: Start the morning with a visit to Mercado de Campo de Ourique — a beloved, authentic local neighborhood market far from the tourist crowds. Browse stalls of fresh produce, artisan cheeses, cured meats, local bread, and seasonal fruits alongside Lisboetas doing their daily shopping. Engage with vendors, sample local products, and absorb the genuine rhythm of Lisbon neighborhood life. This is Lisbon as locals live it.
day_by_day.afternoon: Enjoy a long, leisurely neighborhood lunch at a premium local restaurant near Campo de Ourique — a district known for its charming residential streets and independent eateries. Spend the afternoon exploring the LX Factory, a creative hub in a repurposed 19th-century industrial complex, browsing design boutiques, art galleries, and independent bookshops. Alternatively, visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) for Portugal's finest collection of paintings, silverware, and decorative arts.
day_by_day.evening: For the penultimate evening, indulge in a premium wine-pairing dinner at Tasca do Chico or book a private chef's table experience at Feitoria Restaurant (Michelin-starred, located at the Altis Belém Hotel) — a sophisticated celebration of Portuguese terroir and seasonal ingredients with exceptional river views.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast or a fresh coffee and pastry at a local café in Campo de Ourique — Pastelaria Aloma is a neighborhood institution famous for its custard tarts.
meals.lunch: Tasca da Esquina, Campo de Ourique — Chef Vítor Sobral's acclaimed restaurant celebrating contemporary Portuguese cuisine. €60–90 per person with wine.
meals.dinner: Feitoria Restaurant, Altis Belém Hotel & Spa — tasting menu from €150–180 per person with wine pairing. One Michelin star. Reserve well in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Campo de Ourique market is liveliest on weekend mornings but remains authentic on weekdays. The LX Factory is especially vibrant on Sunday markets — on a Monday, the boutiques and permanent spaces are open but quieter, which can be a pleasant, unhurried experience. Consider booking a private Portuguese wine tasting session in the afternoon as an optional add-on.

day_by_day.morning: On the final morning, revisit a favorite neighborhood or explore Príncipe Real — Lisbon's most elegant and bohemian district, known for its antique shops, gourmet delis, and the beautiful weekend garden market. Browse Embaixada, a stunning neo-Moorish palace converted into a concept store celebrating Portuguese design and craftsmanship — perfect for premium last-minute gifts and souvenirs. Enjoy a slow farewell breakfast at a café overlooking the garden square.
day_by_day.afternoon: Spend the early afternoon at leisure — consider a private rooftop terrace lunch with Tagus views, or return to a beloved spot from earlier in the trip. If time allows before departure logistics, visit the Carmo Archaeological Museum (ruins of a Gothic convent destroyed in the 1755 earthquake — hauntingly beautiful and historically significant). Begin packing and preparing for departure.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at The Yeatman (if a day-trip to Porto wasn't taken) or closer to Lisbon, dine at Varanda Restaurant at the Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon — impeccable service, refined Portuguese cuisine, and a fitting luxury farewell to the city. Arrange a private transfer to the airport for your onward journey.

meals.breakfast: Slow breakfast at Café da Garagem or Landeau Chocolate in Príncipe Real — Landeau's single-origin chocolate cake is legendary and a must before leaving Lisbon.
meals.lunch: Bettina & Niccolò Corallo in Príncipe Real for premium chocolate and light bites, or a final petiscos spread at Taberna da Rua das Flores — one of Lisbon's finest traditional tascas. €50–70 per person.
meals.dinner: Varanda Restaurant, Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon, Rua Rodrigo da Fonseca 88 — refined Portuguese tasting menu from €100–150 per person. Elegant, unhurried, and a worthy farewell to Lisbon.

day_by_day.notes: Allow ample time for the airport transfer — Lisbon traffic can be unpredictable, especially during evening rush hours. A private luxury transfer is strongly recommended for the final departure. Consider purchasing a bottle of aged Vintage Port or a premium Douro red wine as a keepsake from one of Príncipe Real's specialist wine shops.
